title: The Liar Paradox in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy

summaries.example: Imagine a sign that says, “This sign is false.” If the sign is telling the truth, then it must be false. But if it is false, then what it says seems true. Philosophers studied this puzzling loop and tried different ways to explain what has gone wrong.
summaries.summary: The Liar paradox is a puzzle about a sentence such as “This saying is false.” If it is true, then it says it is false. If it is false, then it seems to be true. Philosophers in the Arabic and Islamic world examined this puzzle in many ways. Early writers sometimes treated it as a logical trick or as an example in debates about good and evil. Later writers made it a regular topic in logic and suggested different answers. Some argued that a sentence cannot properly talk about itself. Others said truth requires a statement and the thing it describes to be separate. Still others treated the puzzle as if it contained two statements. The source explains that these thinkers did not all agree, and some solutions faced serious questions. The history shows how one short sentence led to careful thinking about language, truth, and what counts as a statement.
key_ideas: The Liar paradox can begin with a sentence such as “This saying is false.”
A statement that talks about itself can create a loop between truth and falsehood.
Thinkers in the Arabic and Islamic philosophical tradition offered many different solutions.
Some said the puzzling sentence is not really a proper statement, while others said it has no truth value.
The puzzle was discussed from about the tenth through the fifteenth centuries, and later scholars continued discussing it.
summaries.why_it_matters: The puzzle teaches us to look closely at language. A sentence may look ordinary while creating trouble because it talks about itself. Studying the different answers also shows that philosophers can disagree thoughtfully: they may change the meaning of “true,” “false,” or even “statement” to understand the problem better. The discussion is part of the history of logic in Arabic and Islamic philosophy.

important_terms.definition: A puzzle in which a statement seems to make itself both true and false.
A sentence that says something, rather than asking a question or giving an order.
When a statement, word, or idea points back to itself.
Being correct about how things are.
Being incorrect about how things are.

questions_to_think_about: Can a sentence safely tell us whether it is true or false?
Is a sentence always either true or false?
What might be wrong with a sentence that talks about itself?
Which solution seems most helpful: calling the sentence false, or saying it is not a proper statement?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence “This sentence is false.” Suppose it is true. Then what it says must hold, so it is false. Suppose instead that it is false. Then its claim that it is false appears correct, so it is true. The familiar two-step loop is not merely a word game: it raises questions about whether every declarative must be either true or false and whether a declarative can successfully refer to itself.
summaries.summary: The entry traces treatments of the Liar paradox in Arabic and Islamic philosophy from roughly the tenth to the fifteenth century. In its simplest form, the paradox arises when a declarative says of itself that it is false. Truth makes the statement false, while falsehood seems to make it true. Early discussions were not uniform: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAdī treated the puzzle as a sophism involving the different roles of a declarative and its “declared-about”; other early writers used liar-like cases in theological arguments about good and evil; and al-Fārābī and al-Rāzī discussed self-falsifying claims, with al-Rāzī connecting the topic more directly to the Liar. In the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the Liar became a standard logical problem. Al-Abharī and al-Kātibī argued that the Liar is false by analyzing the inference from its falsity to its truth. Al-Ṭūsī argued that self-reference prevents truth or falsehood because correspondence and non-correspondence require distinct relata. Al-Samarqandī analyzed the case as involving two mutually connected evaluations, and al-Taftāzānī developed a temporal Liar cycle while ultimately admitting that his proposed solution was inadequate. Fifteenth-century discussions by al-Dashtakī and al-Dawānī gave further accounts of defective or nonexistent declaratives and of the impossibility of self-imitation. The entry presents these proposals as historically important attempts, not as a settled single solution.
key_ideas: The Arabic tradition developed through several stages: early isolated treatments, more systematic discussions in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and major debates in the fifteenth century.
The standard example changed over time, moving from “All my sayings are false” toward “All my sayings at this moment are false,” and later often toward “This saying is false.”

Because many thinkers held that truth and falsehood are not simple contradictories for every kind of expression, they could allow that non-declaratives or nonexistent declaratives are neither true nor false. They still had to explain why this solves, or fails to solve, the Liar.
Yaḥyā ibn ʿAdī distinguished a declarative from a declarative treated as the subject of another declarative. Al-Ṭūsī instead connected truth and falsehood with correspondence between distinct things.
Al-Samarqandī and al-Taftāzānī explored analyses involving two judgments, while al-Taftāzānī also introduced a temporal Liar cycle.
In the fifteenth century, al-Dashtakī and al-Dawānī offered competing accounts involving missing declaratives, self-reference, and the impossibility or failure of self-imitation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Liar exposes assumptions that are easy to overlook: that every declarative has a truth value, that truth and falsehood exhaust the possibilities, that a sentence can refer to itself, and that truth consists in correspondence with what is described. The Arabic and Islamic tradition is especially valuable because it preserves a long sequence of distinct analyses and criticisms. It also shows that the history of logic includes debates about grammar, theological reasoning, reference, and the structure of judgment, not only formal symbols.

important_terms.definition: A sentence that generates a contradiction by attributing falsehood to itself, or by a closely related self-referential structure.
A saying that presents something as the case and is therefore the kind of saying that may be true or false.
The relation in which a declarative refers to or concerns an object, fact, or another declarative; the source calls these objects its “declared-abouts.”
A statement’s referring to or applying something to itself.
The view that falsehood is non-truth rather than simple negation of truth. On this view, some things can be neither true nor false.
The relation between a declarative and what it is about, used by some thinkers to explain truth and falsehood.
A chain in which statements made at different times refer to one another’s truth or falsehood, producing a Liar-style puzzle.
A saying that creates or performs a fact rather than reporting a fact, contrasted in the source with a declarative.

questions_to_think_about: Does saying that a self-referential sentence has no truth value avoid the paradox, or does it conflict with the definition of a declarative?
Why might correspondence require a declarative and what it is about to be distinct?
Is “All my sayings are false” paradoxical in ordinary conversation, or only under a special assumption about what else the speaker says?
Does treating the Liar as two connected declaratives explain the puzzle, or merely redescribe it?
What is the difference between a sentence that reports a fact and an utterance that helps create a fact?

summaries.example: Suppose a student writes one note on a board: “Everything I am saying right now is false.” If the note is true, then it must be false. If it is false, then not everything it says is false, which seems to make it true. But the puzzle depends on a special setup: the student must be saying only this one thing, or the sentence must clearly include itself. Without that setup, the sentence might simply be false because the student has said something else that is true.
summaries.summary: The Liar paradox is usually introduced with a sentence like “This saying is false.” Its difficulty comes from a loop: if the sentence is true, it is false; if it is false, it appears true. The source follows how philosophers working in Arabic and Islamic contexts discussed this problem from the tenth through the fifteenth centuries. Early authors did not always present the same puzzle. Some used a person who says “I am a liar,” although that phrase can mean different things. Others discussed claims such as “Everything is false,” which are self-refuting but do not become paradoxes unless extra conditions are added. By the thirteenth century, the Liar was a regular topic in logic. Al-Abharī and al-Kātibī argued that the Liar is false and tried to show that the reasoning from falsehood back to truth contains a mistake. Al-Ṭūsī argued that truth and falsehood require a relation between distinct things, so a self-referential declarative cannot receive either value. Al-Samarqandī treated the case as involving two connected judgments, while al-Taftāzānī developed a cycle in which today’s and tomorrow’s statements refer to each other. Later, al-Dashtakī and al-Dawānī proposed that the Liar fails to be a proper declarative because something needed for reference or imitation is missing. The entry records a debate with several competing solutions and unresolved difficulties.
key_ideas: The source distinguishes an ordinary self-refuting claim from a full paradox. “All my sayings are false” becomes paradoxical only under a special condition about the speaker’s other sayings.
In the thirteenth century, the Liar became a standard logical problem often described as the conjunction of two contradictories.
Different philosophers proposed different diagnoses: the Liar may be false, neither true nor false, not a genuine declarative, or a confused combination of judgments.
Some solutions focus on the structure of language. Others focus on truth as correspondence between distinct things.
The tradition includes theological uses of liar-like examples, including arguments about good and evil, but not every example involving a liar is the Liar paradox itself.
By the fifteenth century, al-Dashtakī and al-Dawānī were debating detailed accounts of what a statement refers to and whether a statement can imitate or describe itself.
summaries.why_it_matters: The Liar is a useful test for theories of language and reasoning. It asks whether truth and falsehood are always opposites, whether every meaningful declarative must have one of those values, and whether a statement can describe itself without creating trouble. Following the historical debate also broadens our picture of philosophy: scholars connected logic with grammar, theology, theories of judgment, and the difference between reporting a fact and creating one through speech.

important_terms.definition: A puzzle where a statement seems to force itself to be both true and false.
A sentence that makes a claim and can normally be judged true or false.
A sentence’s referring to itself, as when “this sentence” refers to the sentence being spoken.
The thing that a declarative is about, which may be another statement or a fact.
The idea that a statement is true when it matches what it is about, and false when it does not.
A series of statements made at different times that refer to one another’s truth or falsehood.
A claim that defeats itself, such as “Everything is false,” because accepting it makes it false.

questions_to_think_about: Why does the “only statement” condition matter in the example “All my sayings are false”?
Should a sentence that has no truth value count as a declarative?
Would banning self-reference solve the Liar, or would it also rule out harmless sentences such as “This sentence has seven words”?
What is the difference between saying that an argument is invalid and saying that its conclusion is false?
Which seems more promising: changing the theory of truth or changing the theory of what counts as a statement?
